meta.title: Strata-RAG — decisions and method · Nikolai Sachok
meta.description: The decision record behind Strata-RAG: what I chose, what I rejected, and the four times the system proved me wrong. Every claim carries how strongly it is evidenced.
meta.og_description: What I chose, what I rejected, and the four times the system proved me wrong — each claim graded measured, verified, or reasoned.

lead_1: An eval-first RAG engine, built to be measured rather than demonstrated. It indexes heterogeneous corpora, retrieves with a hybrid of dense and lexical search, and scores retrieval and generation as two separate questions — because one end-to-end number tells you that answer quality moved without telling you which half moved it.
lead_2: What follows is the decision record and the method record: what I chose, what I rejected, and the four times the system proved me wrong. Every entry carries how strongly it is evidenced, because a claim without its grade is only a claim.

bands.label: Decisions
bands.note: Recorded as what I chose, what I rejected, and the conditions under which I would choose differently. A decision with no stated alternative is a preference.

records.title: Fuse dense and lexical retrieval by rank, not by score
records.body: Dense retrieval captures meaning and blurs exact tokens — rare names, identifiers, codes. BM25 nails the exact term and misses the paraphrase. Each covers the other's blind spot, so the real question is how to combine two ranked lists whose scores live on incomparable scales. You cannot add a cosine score to a BM25 score. Reciprocal-rank fusion sidesteps the problem entirely by using rank position only, summing 1/(k+rank), which is also why it needs one parameter instead of a calibration step.

facets.label: Over
facets.text: Dense-only, which is the default in most tutorials and fails silently on exact-term queries. Weighted score fusion, which needs per-retriever normalisation and is fragile. Learned fusion, which is more infrastructure than this corpus earns.

facets.label: Choose differently when
facets.text: The corpus is pure prose with no codes, identifiers or rare names — dense-only may be enough, and there is a --dense-only flag to measure exactly that.

records.rule: This is a reasoned design choice, not a measured result. The dense-only versus hybrid A/B on the real corpus has not been run, and running it is the missing evidence that would let the claim carry a number.

records.title: Rerank with a cross-encoder, behind a flag that can turn it off
records.body: Dense and BM25 are both bi-encoders: the query and the document are embedded separately, so the query never sees the document. A cross-encoder scores the pair together and orders the shortlist far more accurately. Retrieving broadly and reranking about twenty candidates buys corpus-scale recall and pair-scale precision, which is cheap precision for a second model load.

facets.label: Over
facets.text: No reranking, which is fewer moving parts and a worse final ordering. An LLM reranker, which is the highest quality available and costs a per-query model call, the latency that comes with it, and a fresh injection surface on untrusted chunk text.

facets.label: Choose differently when
facets.text: Latency is the binding constraint and the embedder already ranks well — the flag exists for that. Quality is critical and the budget allows an LLM reranker, with injection guards on the chunk text.

records.title: Bound the context with top-k and an absolute score floor — never top-p
records.body: Retrieval needs a bounded context budget, so a fixed top-k. An optional floor on the rerank score drops weak filler after reranking, and is allowed to return nothing at all so the generator can say it has no relevant context rather than answer from junk. There is deliberately no minimum-one fallback, which would defeat the purpose. Top-p is the wrong instrument here and it is worth being precise about why: nucleus sampling assumes a calibrated probability distribution summing to one. Cross-encoder relevance scores are not probabilities, do not sum to one, and are not comparable across models — a good score from one reranker is not a good score from another. Cumulative-mass thresholding over numbers like that is meaningless, so the floor is absolute, empirically tuned per reranker, and off by default.

facets.label: Over
facets.text: Fixed top-k alone, which is the simpler default and keeps the tail. Top-p, which is inapplicable for the reason above. Dynamic k by score gap, which is a brittle heuristic.

facets.label: Choose differently when
facets.text: Precision matters more than recall and you have measured a threshold for your own reranker. Otherwise leave the floor off — a hard-coded universal threshold would mean nothing.

records.title: Run a real vector server, not an in-process store
records.body: An enterprise-shaped engine wants a standalone ANN service: a process several services can point at, inspect over HTTP, tune with explicit HNSW parameters, and grow past in-process memory. Qdrant costs one docker compose up of operational overhead and gives all of that. An embedded store is excellent for a notebook and is not the shape of a production index.

facets.label: Over
facets.text: Chroma, embedded and simplest, but in-process. pgvector, superb when the data already lives in Postgres and you want one transactional store, weaker at pure ANN ergonomics. Pinecone, zero-ops and managed, at the cost of a hosted dependency and data leaving your boundary. Weaviate or Milvus, powerful and distributed, heavier to operate than a single-node engine needs.

facets.label: Choose differently when
facets.text: It is a throwaway notebook — Chroma. The data is already in Postgres at modest scale — pgvector. There is no ops appetite — a managed service. Billions of vectors — a distributed cluster.

records.title: Split PII into a policy and a detector, then make only the detector pluggable
records.body: Redaction is two separable concerns. The policy decides what to keep and what to remove — it keeps published business contacts and role-based addresses, and removes personal ones, using the document's provenance to tell them apart. The detector finds and labels the spans. Keeping them apart means a regex detector ships as the zero-dependency default, and Microsoft Presidio's NER drops in behind an unchanged policy for teams that need free-text coverage. A comparison harness runs both over the same corpus under the same policy and reports the disagreements, with every value masked.

facets.label: Over
facets.text: Regex only, which is blind to names in free text. NER always on, which forces a heavy dependency and a model download onto everyone including the demo. A hosted PII API, which sends the data you are protecting outside your boundary.

facets.label: Choose differently when
facets.text: The PII has known structured shapes — regex is higher precision and cheaper. There are names and phone numbers in prose — Presidio, with the larger model in production. Regulated and on-premise — Presidio locally, never a hosted API.

records.rule: On the sample corpus the regex detector found one email; Presidio found the same email plus thirty PERSON spans regex is structurally unable to see — and also tagged some brand and theme words as people, which is the false-positive cost of the probabilistic backend stated rather than hidden.

bands.label: Method
bands.note: Four times the system proved me wrong, and what each one changed. Measured means a number from a run that can be repeated. Verified means reproduced and confirmed, but not numeric. Reasoned means argued for and not yet measured.

records.title: I built the red team that broke my own injection scanner
records.body: The deterministic scanner matched on the bytes as delivered, so any encoding it had not anticipated was invisible to it. Ninety-three per cent of obfuscated payloads walked straight past. The fix was a normalisation pre-pass: scan a normalised copy — NFKC fold, strip zero-width characters, un-map homoglyphs, bounded base64, morse and rot13 decode — while still delivering the original bytes to the target. Scanner evasion fell from 93% to 17%, end-to-end attack success from 58% to 8%, and six fold-and-decode encoder families from 100% to zero. The normaliser was promoted into the engine as a shared component so the scanner and the red team cannot drift apart.
records.rule: The residual 17% is published rather than buried. A security number without its remainder is marketing.

records.title: A jailbreak score with no denominator is a coin flip in a suit
records.body: Live testing found the same zero-width payload hijacking the model in six of eight trials and refusing once. Model compliance is stochastic, so a single-shot attack-success rate is not a measurement of anything. The harness now fires each payload N times and reports a per-payload success rate, with errors — timeouts, 502s — excluded from the denominator, because a failed request is not a refusal and counting it as one flatters the defence. Scanner evasion stays deterministic and single-shot, because that layer genuinely is a function of the bytes.
records.rule: Separate the parts of a security metric that are deterministic from the parts that are sampled, and never report them on the same scale.

records.title: The judge that decides whether an attack succeeded went through five rewrites and ended by giving up on words
records.body: The oracle's job sounds trivial — did the model comply? — and every lexical approach died on a reproduced counter-example. Whole-answer substring matching scored a refusal that quotes the canary as a hijack. A proximity window fixed that and introduced cross-clause false negatives. Per-span negation scoping fixed those and still over-reported on quoted needles inside code fences. A uniform refusal-taint rule was sound and leaked on the alerting register, where modern refusals contain no hard negation word at all. So the deterministic path was made lexicon-free and structural-only: it fires only on forms a refusal physically cannot produce. Everything else is ambiguous and routed to a behavioural judge, or scored conservatively when no judge is available.
records.rule: A negation lexicon is an unbounded arms race. The layer now errs in one direction only, which makes a deterministic-only score a documented lower bound and never a false all-clear — and every one of the eleven false positives and two false negatives found along the way is now a permanent regression test.

records.title: Some production documents contain live credentials, and indexing them turns retrieval into exfiltration
records.body: Ingest-time redaction — entropy scoring plus contextual key detection — caught and removed 174 live credentials from a large heterogeneous production corpus before a single chunk was embedded. Once a secret is in the vector store it is retrievable, quotable and effectively undeletable. Two structural points sit behind the number. Secret redaction is a separate pass from PII redaction and runs first, so an email-and-password pair is recognised as a credential rather than anonymised into a harmless-looking address. And the structured metadata harvest reads per-project config files that are never embedded at all, through a field whitelist rather than a blocklist.
records.rule: Fail closed. A whitelist excludes the secret block a future config file has not introduced yet; a blocklist only excludes the ones you already thought of.
